steps.prompt: Imagine your backpack is in a pile of thirty backpacks. Describe it in one sentence so a stranger could find it.

cards.title: Zoom in
cards.body: Good description picks details only this object has. Not “a blue backpack” (there are ten of those), but “a faded blue backpack with a broken zip and a keyring shaped like a taco”. Size, colour, texture, smell, sound, age and damage are all clues.

cards.title: Choose, don’t pile
cards.body: Two exact adjectives beat five vague ones. “The big, huge, enormous truck” says less than “the enormous truck”. If two words mean the same thing, keep the stronger one.

cards.title: Compare to make it clear
cards.text:
The trophy is smaller than my hand.
It is the oldest thing on my shelf.
The gold paint is more chipped on one side.
cards.note: Comparisons give the reader something to measure against. “Small” is vague; “smaller than my hand” is exact.

cards.title: Adverbs set the scene
cards.text: Every morning I carefully zip it shut and hang it upstairs.
cards.note: When (every morning), how (carefully) and where (upstairs) show how the object fits into your life.

prompts: Which detail in your description would help a stranger most? Why?
Did you cut any describing words while you revised? Which ones, and why?
